_what: Synthetic ownership-reconciliation gate, following bench/dart-closure-binders: exact cells and fingerprints of what reconcileOwnership registers, a scaling ratio against input and output growth, and a count of the registry entries the pass is handed. Real TypeScript scope extractor and populateOwners, real reconcileOwnership and SemanticModel; the rest of scope resolution, analyze and persistence are outside this benchmark.
_triage: Shape and fingerprint failures are deterministic: inspect the corpus and the registry contents, never rebaseline just to make CI green. The runner also fails, before any baseline comparison, when a shared bucket does not hold exactly one def per file or the second pass registers anything. An operation-count failure is deterministic too: the pass was handed more registry entries per def as the shared buckets grew, so something reads a long bucket from the registry per def again. The count only sees reads through lookupAllByOwner; a per-def scan of some other copy of a bucket is caught by the timing ratio alone. For a timing failure, the report's estimator block shows the profile and the rounds taken (ci: 25 interleaved samples after 3 warmups; full: 75 after 5; a ratio over budget is sampled for up to 3 rounds before it fails): rerun on an idle machine before investigating a regression. Millisecond observations are context, not gates.
_shape_note: Exact counts are the workload FLOOR. small = 250 files, large = 1000 files (files 4x). Each file declares the module-level values logger, router and config and a top-level interface Options with one member, level; the index in each file is zero-padded to a fixed width, so input bytes grow exactly 4x. The three values and every Options are ownerless, so each of the four shared buckets ends up holding one def per file; Options.level is owned, one def per owner. first_pass registers into a fresh model, second_pass reconciles the same files again and must register nothing.
_fingerprint_note: Recorded on main ef126ea20. Identical for a plain bucket scan, for a node-id set per key, and for the scan-then-set check the pass uses now: none of them alters a registration. Hashes pin every (registry, owner, name) key the workload's defs map to and the node ids under it, in registry order. The workload never repeats a def within one pass; the unit tests cover that case.
_scaling_note: The scaling ratio is (t_large / t_small) / growth, where growth is the larger of the input-byte, def and registry-entry growth between the two cells (4 here): about 1 is linear, about 4 is quadratic at these sizes. Budget 1.5, as in bench/scope-capture and bench/dart-closure-binders. Under --check a ratio over the budget is sampled again, up to 3 rounds of the profile's samples, and the minimum is taken over all of them; the budget itself does not move.
_operations_note: Outside the timed passes, a wrapper around each registry's lookupAllByOwner adds up the length of every bucket a read hands back, taken at the moment of the read (a registry returns its live bucket). It is an upper bound on the entries the pass compares through the registry. The pass scans a bucket while it holds at most 8 defs and reads it once more into a node-id set when it grows past that, so a shared bucket costs a fixed 45 entries in the pass that fills it and one full read in a later pass, whatever the file count. A scan per def reads the whole shared bucket for every def, so the count per def grows with the file count. The ratio between the cells is gated at 1.1. It is a count, so it fails deterministically whatever the timings say.
_size_note: The shapes are small on purpose. A pass costs well under a microsecond per def, mostly hash probes into tables that grow with the file count, so once the large shape's tables leave a cache level the small shape still sits in, per-def time rises with no change in the work done: a plain loop doing the same probes read 1.5-1.8 at 1000 vs 4000 files on a loaded host, and the linear pass read 1.3-1.6 there. At 250 vs 1000 both cells sit in the same regime and the bucket scan still reads about 4.
_negative_controls_note: Making the pass scan every bucket (no node-id sets) keeps every shape and fingerprint identical and fails both gates under --check: 'reconcile_files_scaling_ratio: 4.636740799642482 > 1.5 (min of 75 samples)' and 'registry_entries_read_files_scaling_ratio: 4.002001334222816 > 1.1'. The scan was handed 374750 registry entries for the small cell and 5999000 for the large one (299.8 and 1199.8 per def) against 1430 and 5180 (1.14 and 1.04 per def) with the scan-then-set check.
_profiles_note: Two profiles share the shapes and every accuracy gate. CI (the default, and what --check runs in the benchmarks job): one process, every workload timed interleaved in rotating order, min of 25 after 3 warmups. --full: min of 75 after 5 warmups. A sample takes milliseconds, so the sample count is higher than in the parse-worker gates at no real cost. Under --check a timing ratio over budget adds another round of samples, up to 3 rounds. Build-free: no parse worker, no dist/.

_measured_ci.environment: Linux x64 (i9-12900K, 24 logical cores) / Node 22.23.3, 2026-11-14, shared host (load average about 4 to 9 during these runs)
_measured_ci.timing_gate_under_load: 30 --check runs alternated with 30 single-round runs while 18 busy loops ran alongside on 24 cores: 6 single-round runs exceeded 1.5 (highest 1.788); with up to 3 rounds 1 did (1.877), and 5 passes needed more than one round.

_measured_note: Two CI-profile --check runs with the scan-then-set check (both PASS) and one with every bucket scanned (FAIL on both gates). Exact shapes and fingerprints are identical in all three.
